entries_new.name: Chile independence referendum, 1817
entries_new.mechanism: A plebiscite called by the head of government, followed by a declaration of independence.
entries_new.story: Chile was a Spanish colony. After the Battle of Chacabuco, Bernardo O'Higgins was appointed director supremo, the head of the new government, and held a plebiscite on 15 November 1817 to test what people wanted. The independence proposal passed by a large majority. His government declared independence on 16 February 1818. Wikipedia's table notes that Chile declared independence unilaterally and lists the result as not recognised at the time.

entries_new.name: Maryland in Africa independence referendum, 1853
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum of settlers, then a constitution and a declaration of independence.
entries_new.story: The Maryland State Colonization Society, a US group, founded the Maryland Colony in Africa on 22 February 1834. After Liberia declared independence in 1847, settlers asked the authorities for a referendum. It was held on 31 January 1853, and only 122 people voted, all for independence. A constitutional council was elected in February 1854, a constitution was approved by referendum in March 1854, and the Republic of Maryland declared independence on 8 June 1854.

entries_new.name: Norway union dissolution referendum, 1905
entries_new.mechanism: A parliamentary declaration endorsed by a national referendum.
entries_new.story: Norway had been in a union with Sweden since 1814. After a dispute over a separate Norwegian consular service, the Storting (parliament) declared on 7 June 1905 that the union had ended. On 13 August 1905 voters were asked to endorse this. Dissolution was approved by 368,208 votes to 184, 99.95 percent of valid votes, on a turnout of 85.4 percent. Only men could vote. Women's groups ran a parallel signature campaign of close to 280,000 names.

entries_new.name: Iceland sovereignty referendum, 1918
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum approving a treaty-like Act of Union with the colonial power.
entries_new.story: On 19 October 1918 Iceland voted on an Act of Union with the Kingdom of Denmark. The Act would make Iceland a separate kingdom under the Danish Crown, a sovereign state in a personal union with Denmark, meaning the two shared a monarch. It was approved by 92.6 percent of voters. Wikipedia's table lists this as a vote for independence that Denmark recognised.

entries_new.name: Cambodia referendum, 1945
entries_new.mechanism: Questions put to voters through provincial governors.
entries_new.story: A six-question referendum was held in Cambodia on 3 October 1945. Questions included whether the country should become independent and whether foreign troops should be refused. There were no no-votes on any question, and turnout was 80.3 percent. Prime Minister Son Ngoc Thanh, who had replaced Ung Hy on 10 August, called it to give his government legitimacy. It is unclear whether ballots were cast in boxes. Thanh sent the questions to provincial governors to put to voters. Wikipedia's table lists France as the power concerned.

entries_new.name: Mongolia independence referendum, 1945
entries_new.recognition: Republic of China (1946, later withdrawn); People's Republic of China
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum required by a Sino-Soviet treaty as the condition for Chinese recognition.
entries_new.story: Outer Mongolia, then the Mongolian People's Republic and a Soviet-aligned state, held an independence referendum on 20 October 1945. Official statistics gave 100 percent in favour with no votes against, and turnout of 98 percent. In the Sino-Soviet Treaty of 14 August 1945 the Republic of China had agreed to recognise Mongolian independence after a successful referendum. In January 1946 the Nationalist government of China recognised it. Wikipedia's table notes that recognition was abolished in 1953, and that the People's Republic of China recognises it.

entries_new.name: Faroe Islands independence referendum, 1946
entries_new.stopped_by: Denmark dissolved the Løgting and called new elections
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum followed by a declaration of independence by the parliament chairman.
entries_new.story: The Faroe Islands are an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. On 14 September 1946 a narrow majority of valid votes (50.7 percent) favoured independence, but invalid votes outnumbered the winning margin. The chairman of the Løgting (the Faroese parliament) declared independence on 18 September. Neither a majority of the Løgting nor the Danish parliament and government accepted this. King Christian X dissolved the Løgting on 24 September, and in the November election parties for full independence received 5,396 votes against 7,488 for the others. Denmark then granted greater self-rule.

entries_new.name: Newfoundland referendums, 1948
entries_new.mechanism: Two referendums run by Britain on the territory's future, with independence as one option.
entries_new.story: Newfoundland, a self-governing Dominion since 1907, fell into debt and was run from 1934 by a Commission of Government with British and local members. Two referendums on 3 June and 22 July 1948 asked voters to choose between continuing the Commission, restoring responsible government (self-rule, which meant independence), and, after Britain overruled the local Convention in March, confederation with Canada. No option won over 50 percent on 3 June, so a second vote followed. Newfoundland joined Canada on 31 March 1949 as its tenth province.

entries_new.name: Cameroon constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 French Cameroons voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 96.6% of voters.

entries_new.name: Ubangi-Shari constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Ubangi-Shari voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 98.77% of voters.

entries_new.name: Chad constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Chad voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 98.29% of voters.

entries_new.name: Comoros constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 the Comoros voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 97.33% of voters.

entries_new.name: Moyen-Congo constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting the new French constitution would have meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Moyen-Congo voted on the new French constitution in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French overseas territories. The constitution made the territory an autonomous republic within the French Community, and 99 percent of voters approved it. The Territorial Assembly proclaimed the Republic of the Congo on 28 November 1958, and the country became independent two years later.

entries_new.name: Dahomey constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Dahomey voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 98% of voters.

entries_new.name: Gabon constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 French Gabon voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 92.6% of voters. Turnout was 78.7 percent.

entries_new.name: Guinea constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A no vote on the French constitution, which under its terms meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Guinea voted on the new French constitution in a referendum held across the French Union and France. Rejecting it meant independence. Guinea's main party, the Democratic Party of Guinea under Ahmed Sekou Toure, campaigned for no, and more than 95 percent voted against, on a turnout of 85.5 percent. Guinea was the only territory to reject the constitution. It declared independence on 2 October. Wikipedia reports that France withdrew totally and halted development assistance, and that relations quickly became strained.

entries_new.name: French Somaliland constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting the new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 French Somaliland, now Djibouti, voted on the new French constitution. Rejecting it meant independence. It was approved by 75.24 percent. Wikipedia says the Afar people and resident Europeans largely voted yes, and most no voters were Somalis who favoured joining a united Somalia, as proposed by Mahmoud Harbi, then Vice President of the Government Council. There were allegations of widespread vote rigging. The UN noted an unusual number of invalid ballots in Somali districts and suggested manipulation.

entries_new.name: French Polynesia constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting the new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 French Polynesia voted on the new French constitution, where rejection meant independence. About 64 percent voted yes. Some members of the Democratic Rally of the Tahitian People, removed from power by the governor in April, backed no, but officials restricted their campaigning, and on some outlying islands voters did not know no was an option. After riots on 10 and 11 October its leader Pouvanaa a Oopa was convicted of arson and exiled to France. A court quashed the conviction in 2018, finding police had fabricated evidence.

entries_new.name: Madagascar constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Madagascar voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 77.64% of voters. The country became independent on 26 June 1960.

entries_new.name: French Sudan constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 French Sudan voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 97.54% of voters.

entries_new.name: Mauritania constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Mauritania voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 94.04% of voters.

entries_new.name: Saint Pierre and Miquelon constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Saint Pierre and Miquelon voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 98% of voters.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1958 Saint Pierre and Miquelon constitutional referendum

entries_new.name: Senegal constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Senegal voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 97.55% of voters.

entries_new.name: Upper Volta constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Upper Volta voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 99.18% of voters.

entries_new.name: Niger constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Niger voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 78% of voters. Wikipedia says the vote was marred by widespread irregularities and manipulation by the colonial administration, aimed at countering Djibo Bakary, who had denounced French economic blackmail and demanded immediate independence.

entries_new.name: New Caledonia constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 New Caledonia voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 98.12% of voters. In August 1958 the leaders of the two main parties, Maurice Lenormand and Georges Chatenay, met Charles de Gaulle and committed to campaign for yes.

entries_new.name: Ivory Coast constitutional referendum, 1958
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in which rejecting a new French constitution meant independence.
entries_new.story: On 28 September 1958 Ivory Coast voted on the new French constitution, in a referendum held across the French Union, the group of French territories overseas. A yes vote made the territory part of the new French Community. A no vote meant independence. It was approved by 99.99% of voters.

entries_new.name: Western Samoa constitution and independence referendums, 1961
entries_new.mechanism: UN-supervised double referendum on a constitution and independence.
entries_new.story: Western Samoa was a New Zealand-administered UN trust territory, taken from Germany in the First World War. A Constitutional Assembly of matai (family chiefs) drafted a constitution in 1960, restricting voting and standing for office to matai. Because of that, the UN insisted on a supervised vote before ending the trusteeship. Two referendums on 10 May 1961 asked about the constitution and about independence from 1 January 1962. Both were approved. New Zealand passed the Western Samoa Act 1961, the UN General Assembly voted unanimously to end the trusteeship, and independence began on 1 January 1962.

entries_new.name: Algeria independence referendum, 1962
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum written into the Evian Accords between France and the FLN.
entries_new.story: The Algerian War began on 1 November 1954 with attacks by the National Liberation Front (FLN). In 1961 a French referendum on self-determination for Algeria passed with 75 percent, and the Evian Accords, signed in March 1962, were approved by 91 percent in France on 8 April. On 1 July 1962 voters in French Algeria were asked whether Algeria should become an independent state cooperating with France. 99.72 percent said yes on a turnout of 91.88 percent. France declared Algeria independent on 3 July, and Algerian leaders marked 5 July as Independence Day.

entries_new.name: Malta constitutional referendum, 1964
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum approving an independence constitution.
entries_new.story: A constitutional referendum was held in Malta from 2 to 4 May 1964. The new constitution was approved by 54.5 percent of voters and came into effect on 21 September 1964. Wikipedia calls it effectively a referendum on independence, because the constitution gave the country self-government. The Progressive Constitutionalist Party led by Mabel Strickland boycotted the vote. The British government is listed as the power Malta separated from.

entries_new.name: Southern Rhodesia independence referendum, 1964
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum largely of white voters, followed by a unilateral declaration of independence.
entries_new.story: On 5 November 1964 voters in the British colony of Southern Rhodesia were asked whether they favoured independence on the basis of the 1961 constitution. More than 90 percent said yes on a turnout of 62 percent, though under 15 percent of the voter roll was black. Prime Minister Ian Smith held an indaba, a meeting, with tribal leaders, but Britain did not treat them as representative, because they were paid by the government. Smith's government issued a Unilateral Declaration of Independence in 1965. Britain did not accept it, and the territory returned to British rule in 1979 after the Lancaster House Agreement.

entries_new.name: French Somaliland independence referendum, 1967
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum ordered by the French president.
entries_new.story: President Charles de Gaulle ordered a vote in French Somaliland on 19 March 1967, after riots during his visit in 1966. The French called it a plebiscite. Voters rejected independence by a 22-point margin. Wikipedia reports vote rigging by French authorities, including about 10,000 Somalis deported on the grounds that they lacked valid identity cards. Official figures put the population at 58,240 Somalis and 48,270 Afars, yet 14,689 Somalis were registered against 22,004 Afars. France denied claims it imported Afar nomads. A third vote in 1977 backed independence.

entries_new.name: Northern Mariana Islands status referendum, 1969
entries_new.mechanism: A local referendum with five options before a UN visit.
entries_new.story: The Northern Mariana Islands, a US-administered territory, held a status referendum on 9 November 1969, organised by the local parliament before a UN commission visited in early 1970. Voters chose from five options. For the fourth time since 1958 a majority supported integration with Guam. Earlier votes on integration or status had been held in 1958, 1961 and 1963, each with a majority for integration, which never happened. Guam had voted on 4 November 1969 and rejected integration with the islands, with 58 percent against. Wikipedia's table records no majority for independence.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1969 Northern Mariana Islands status referendum

entries_new.name: Bahrain independence survey, 1970
entries_new.mechanism: A UN consultation of residents agreed by Britain and Iran.
entries_new.story: In 1970 the United Nations ran a poll in Bahrain on whether islanders preferred independence or Iranian control, sometimes called a referendum. Britain and Iran had both agreed in 1969 to ask the UN to settle the dispute. The UN representative reported that the overwhelming majority wanted a full independent and sovereign state. The Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 278 on 11 May 1970, and that month Iran renounced its claim to the island. Bahrain became independent from the United Kingdom in August 1971.

entries_new.name: Niue constitutional referendum, 1974
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum on a constitution creating free association rather than independence.
entries_new.story: On 3 September 1974 Niue voted on a constitution drafted by Robert Quentin-Baxter, a law professor at Victoria University of Wellington, with the Niue Assembly. It asked about self-government in free association with New Zealand. Niue would become an autonomous region under New Zealand sovereignty, and islanders would receive New Zealand citizenship and the right to settle there. 65 percent approved, and it came into force on 19 October 1974. Wikipedia's table records a majority for associated status, not independence.

entries_new.name: Comoros independence referendum, 1974
entries_new.mechanism: A single territory-wide referendum under a treaty with France.
entries_new.story: A treaty of 15 June 1973 allowed the Comoros to become independent from France within five years after a consultation. France chose one vote for the whole colony instead of island-by-island votes, which Marcel Henry of the Mahoré People's Movement criticised in Mayotte, citing Article 53 of the French Constitution. On 22 December 1974, 94.57 percent voted for independence on a turnout of 93.3 percent. Almost all no votes came from Mayotte. The Comoros declared independence on 6 July 1975, and Mayotte stayed under French control.

entries_new.name: Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands status referendum, 1975
entries_new.mechanism: A six-option referendum across the trust territory.
entries_new.story: The Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, a UN trust territory run by the United States, held a status referendum on 8 July 1975 with six options: independence, commonwealth, free association, statehood, the current status, or another status. In Chuuk, Kosrae, Pohnpei and Yap, later the Federated States of Micronesia, independence led at 59.1 percent, while free association got 58.0 and the present status 59.0. Turnout was 52.6 percent. In the Marshall Islands only keeping the present status was approved, at 77 percent, on turnout of 35.2 percent. In Palau only free association (68 percent) and the present status (78 percent) were approved.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1975 Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands status referendum

entries_new.name: Guam status referendum, 1976
entries_new.mechanism: A territory-wide vote on status options.
entries_new.story: Guam, a US territory, held a referendum on its status on 4 September 1976. Voters were offered a range of options, and an improved status quo received 58 percent. Wikipedia's table lists no majority for independence and Guam remained a US territory.

entries_new.name: Aruba independence referendum, 1977
entries_new.stopped_by: The independence plan was scrapped in 1994
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum followed by a treaty timetable for independence.
entries_new.story: In 1976 the Estates approved a referendum on Aruba's status. It was held on 25 March 1977 and offered independence or staying in the Netherlands Antilles, with over 95 percent voting for the former. The 1983 Treaty of The Hague planned independence for Aruba by 1996, and the island separated from the Netherlands Antilles in 1986. In 1994 the plan for full independence was dropped, and Aruba remained within the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

entries_new.name: Afars and Issas independence referendum, 1977
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum held with an election for a constituent assembly.
entries_new.story: The French Territory of the Afars and the Issas held an independence referendum on 8 May 1977, alongside an election for a Constituent Assembly. Votes in 1958 and 1967 had rejected independence. This one backed it, and the territory became independent as Djibouti on 27 June 1977, a date celebrated each year as Independence Day.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1977 Afars and Issas independence referendum

entries_new.name: Nevis independence referendum, 1977
entries_new.mechanism: An unofficial referendum organised by a party.
entries_new.story: The Nevis Reformation Party organised an unofficial referendum on 18 August 1977 for Nevis to separate from St Kitts before independence and remain a separate British Crown colony, like Anguilla, which had left Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla in 1967. 99.66 percent voted yes, but the national government declared the result invalid. When Saint Kitts and Nevis became independent in 1983, its constitution (Article 113) gave Nevis a right to secede after a referendum with a two-thirds majority. A 1998 vote reached 62 percent and failed.

entries_new.name: Ciskei independence referendum, 1980
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum in a homeland, followed by South African legislation granting nominal independence.
entries_new.story: Ciskei was a Bantustan, a territory set aside by South Africa's government for black South Africans under apartheid. It held an independence referendum on 4 December 1980, and over 99 percent voted yes. Results were announced on 17 December. South Africa passed the Status of Ciskei Act in 1981 and Ciskei was declared independent that year. Wikipedia's table says South Africa recognised it and the rest of the international community did not.

entries_new.name: Guam status referendum, January 1982
entries_new.mechanism: A multi-option status referendum followed by a runoff.
entries_new.story: Guam held a status referendum on 30 January 1982. The option of becoming a US commonwealth received the most votes but not a majority. A second referendum with only two options was therefore held in September. Wikipedia's table lists no majority for independence and Guam remained a US territory.

entries_new.name: Falkland Islands sovereignty survey, 1986
entries_new.mechanism: A postal questionnaire to registered voters.
entries_new.story: An unofficial status referendum was held in the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1986. It took the form of a questionnaire sent to all registered voters by the Falkland Islands Association and the Marplan Institute, called the Falkland Island Sovereignty Survey. 96 percent favoured continued British sovereignty, and 88 percent of registered voters took part. Marplan released the results on 2 April.

entries_new.name: New Caledonia independence referendum, 1987
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum with a three-year residence franchise, boycotted by independence movements.
entries_new.story: A French law passed on 15 April 1984 by 325 votes to 249 provided for an independence referendum in New Caledonia, after the Socialist government recognised Kanak rights to self-determination in 1983. Under President Jacques Chirac, all French citizens who had lived in the territory for three years could vote, which left the indigenous Kanak a minority of voters. Independence movements including the Kanak and Socialist National Liberation Front boycotted the 13 September 1987 vote. Only 1.7 percent voted for independence.

entries_new.name: Slovenia independence referendum, 1990
entries_new.mechanism: A plebiscite with a turnout threshold set by parliament.
entries_new.story: On 23 December 1990 the Republic of Slovenia, then part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, asked voters: should Slovenia become an independent and sovereign state? The ruling coalition and the opposition both backed yes. Parliament set a validity threshold of 50 percent plus one of all registered voters. Of 1,457,020 eligible, 88.5 percent of registered voters (95.7 percent of those taking part) voted yes, 4 percent no. Final results were proclaimed on 26 December. Wikipedia's table lists the result as leading to independence.

entries_new.name: Armenia independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum following a declaration of sovereignty.
entries_new.story: The Armenian SSR held an independence referendum on 21 September 1991 to decide whether to leave the Soviet Union. It followed a declaration of state sovereignty by the Supreme Soviet on 23 August 1990, after a non-Communist government under Levon Ter-Petrosyan took office. 99.5 percent voted yes on a turnout of 95 percent, and Armenia became an independent state on 23 September 1991. The government had rejected Gorbachev's proposed all-Union referendum.

entries_new.name: Azerbaijan independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum on a constitutional act of independence.
entries_new.story: A referendum was held in Azerbaijan on 29 December 1991, three days after the Soviet Union collapsed. 99.8 percent voted for a constitutional act on the independence of the Republic of Azerbaijan, and reported turnout was 95 percent. Wikipedia's table lists the result as leading to independence.

entries_new.name: Palau Compact of Free Association referendum, 1984
entries_new.mechanism: A two-question referendum on a treaty of free association.
entries_new.story: A first referendum in Palau on a Compact of Free Association with the United States had failed to reach the 75 percent needed. A second was held on 4 September 1984 with two questions: whether to approve the Compact, and, if it was rejected, whether voters wanted a closer relationship than trusteeship or independence. The Compact was approved by 67.1 percent, which made the second question irrelevant, though 3,378 blank ballots exceeded either choice. Turnout was 71.3 percent. Wikipedia's table lists no majority for independence.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1984 Palauan Compact of Free Association referendum

entries_new.name: Croatia independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum followed by a declaration and a pause under international pressure.
entries_new.story: Croatia held an independence referendum on 19 May 1991 as Yugoslavia was breaking up. Turnout was 83 percent and 93 percent voted for independence. Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991, then accepted a three-month moratorium (a pause) urged by the European Community under the Brioni Agreement. The war in Croatia escalated during that pause, and on 8 October 1991 the Croatian Parliament cut all remaining ties with Yugoslavia. In 1992 the European Economic Community countries recognised Croatia and it joined the United Nations.

entries_new.name: Estonia independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum on restoring a state that existed before Soviet annexation.
entries_new.story: A referendum in the Estonian SSR on 3 March 1991, held the same day as one in Latvia, asked: do you want the restoration of the national independence and sovereignty of the Republic of Estonia? It was approved by 78 percent of voters on an 83 percent turnout. The Estonian Supreme Council restored independence on the night of 20 August 1991.

entries_new.name: Georgia independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum on restoring the 1918 independence declaration.
entries_new.story: On 31 March 1991 the Republic of Georgia voted on whether to restore the independence declared on 26 May 1918. The Supreme Council, elected in October 1990 and led by a pro-independence bloc under Zviad Gamsakhurdia, called the vote. Official results gave over 99 percent in favour on a 90.6 percent turnout. The non-Georgian population in Abkhazia and South Ossetia largely boycotted it. Four days after the final results the Supreme Council passed a declaration of independence.

entries_new.name: Kosovo independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: An underground assembly declared independence, followed by a referendum.
entries_new.story: Kosovo was then the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo. Its Provincial Assembly, dissolved by Serbian authorities in 1989 but still meeting underground through its Albanian members, declared the Republic of Kosova sovereign and independent on 22 September 1991. A referendum from 26 to 30 September had over 99 percent in favour on 87 percent turnout, needing at least 66.7 percent turnout. Serbs, about 10 percent of the population, boycotted. Only Albania recognised the republic, by a parliamentary resolution on 21 October 1991.

entries_new.name: Latvia independence poll, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A popular survey held on the same day as Estonia's referendum.
entries_new.story: The Popular Survey about the independence of the Republic of Latvia took place on 3 March 1991 in the Latvian SSR, the same day as Estonia's. Voters were asked whether they favoured a democratic and independent Republic of Latvia. It was approved by 74.9 percent on an 87.6 percent turnout. Latvian civilians registered in Soviet Army units could also vote. Independence was restored on 21 August 1991.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Latvian independence and democracy poll, 1991

entries_new.name: Lithuania independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.recognition: United States (2 Sept 1991); Soviet Union (6 Sept 1991)
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum confirming an earlier declaration.
entries_new.story: Lithuania held a referendum on 9 February 1991, eleven months after it declared independence from the Soviet Union on 11 March 1990. Just over 93 percent of those voting said yes, and 76.5 percent of all eligible voters did, far above the 50 percent threshold. Independence was achieved in August 1991. The United States re-recognised it on 2 September 1991 and the Soviet Union on 6 September 1991.

entries_new.name: Macedonia independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum called after other Yugoslav republics left.
entries_new.story: Macedonia, now North Macedonia, held a referendum on 8 September 1991 asking: are you for a sovereign and independent state of Macedonia, with a right to enter into any future alliance with the sovereign states of Yugoslavia? 96 percent approved on 76 percent turnout. Most ethnic Albanians boycotted because of the second half of the question. The parliament had called it in August after Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in June. 8 September is Independence Day.

entries_new.name: Ukraine independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum confirming a parliamentary declaration.
entries_new.story: On 1 December 1991 Ukraine held a referendum asking: do you confirm the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine? The Verkhovna Rada had adopted the Act on 24 August 1991, after the failed August coup and the New Union Treaty going unsigned. 31,891,742 voters, 84.18 percent, took part, and 28,804,071, or 92.3 percent, voted yes. A presidential election on the same day was won by Leonid Kravchuk. From 2 December 1991 other countries recognised Ukraine as independent.

entries_new.name: Uzbekistan independence referendum, 1991
entries_new.mechanism: A referendum held after independence was already declared.
entries_new.story: Uzbekistan held an independence vote on 29 December 1991, alongside presidential elections and three days after the Soviet Union broke up. 98 percent voted yes on a turnout of 94 percent. In the March 1991 Soviet-wide referendum, 95 percent in the Uzbek SSR had voted to keep a renewed union. After the failed August coup, which the Uzbek leadership had endorsed, independence was declared on 31 August. It was the only republic to hold an independence referendum after the Union ended, having already declared independence while it still existed.
